title: Laetare Sunday
hook: the rose vestments again, halfway through Lent

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Annunciation: a question, an answer, and your line, be it done. Did you stop at noon and remember Nazareth? Day six hundred fifty-seven.

Anyone who has run a long race knows the halfway marker. Your legs hurt, your enthusiasm from the start line is gone, and the finish is still a long way off. Then a sign, a water table, someone on the curb cheering, and you find a little more. Lent has one too. On its fourth Sunday, for one day, the violet gives way to rose. If you were with us back in Advent on Gaudete Sunday, you've seen this color before. It shows up only twice a year, and both times it means the same thing.

Laetare is Latin for rejoice, said to one: to a city. It's the first word of the old entrance chant for the fourth Sunday of Lent, from the last chapter of Isaiah. In the Douay-Rheims: "Rejoice with Jerusalem, and be glad with her, all you that love her." Isaiah wrote to people who had mourned Jerusalem's ruin, promising that the city would be like a mother again, nursing and comforting her children. The Church picked that verse for the middle of Lent, when the fasting starts to feel long, the resolutions are wobbling, and Easter is still out of sight. So for one day, the color lightens. Flowers, which are usually left off the altar in Lent, may come back. The organ, often quieter in Lent, can play more freely. It's sometimes called Mid-Lent Sunday, and in England and Ireland it's also Mothering Sunday, a day people once traveled to their mother church, the cathedral or the parish of their baptism, and which later became a day to honor mothers too. In some years, the gospel is the prodigal son, the story with a feast for the one who came home. In others it's the man born blind, who sees. Both are stories where the long darkness breaks. Rome kept a custom too: on this Sunday popes would bless a golden rose, an ornament of gold sometimes given to a church or a person as an honor. Gaudete in Advent, Laetare in Lent. One comes in the dark of December, one as Lent's fasting starts to drag, and each time the color tells the people in the pews how far they've already come.
screen: `LAETARE: REJOICE, O CITY.` · `JERUSALEM LIKE A MOTHER.` · `FLOWERS AND ORGAN RETURN.` · `GAUDETE AND LAETARE.` · then, large: `REJOICE WITH JERUSALEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take a breath of joy. Sit, and breathe in slowly, as though you're breathing in something good: fresh air, morning, coffee, the smell of rain. Hold it a moment. Breathe out whatever has felt heavy this Lent, or this month. Do that a few times. Then name one thing you're honestly glad about today, however small. Let it be enough. If you pray, you can say Isaiah's word, rejoice. If you don't, just let the gladness have a minute. The bell holds the time.
Laetare. Latin for rejoice; the fourth Sunday of Lent, halfway to Easter, with rose vestments. Today's word.
Your line: halfway, rejoice. Today, if you're in the middle of something long, celebrate the halfway point out loud. Day six hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: On the fourth Sunday of Lent the priest may wear rose vestments instead of violet, and the entrance antiphon begins with Isaiah 66:10, Laetare, Jerusalem.

what it means: Laetare Sunday, the halfway point of Lent, when the Church lightens the color and says rejoice.
what a scholar hears: the introit 'Laetare, Ierusalem' takes Isaiah 66:10; the day was also called Mid-Lent and Mothering Sunday, and popes blessed the golden rose.

notes: Flowers on the altar and freer use of the organ permitted on Laetare Sunday (GIRM 305, 313). Confirm.
Mothering Sunday's origin as a visit to the 'mother church' is the standard account; confirm.
Golden Rose blessed by popes on Laetare Sunday; current practice is occasional. Script uses past tense. Confirm.
Prodigal son (Year C) and man born blind (Year A) as Laetare gospels; Year B is John 3:14–21. Confirm the 'in some years ... in others' framing.
